child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 2 months, would like support with the baby's language (talking and singing to the bump).
activity_description: Invite the baby's father and other close family members to take turns talking, reading or singing to the baby during pregnancy, for example in the evening when people are at home. Speak softly about what is happening that day, and pause to notice any movement in reply.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 2 months, would like support with the baby's language (talking and singing to the bump).
activity_name: Telling the Baby About Your Day
activity_description: While you cook, walk or rest, describe what you are doing out loud to the baby: what you are cooking, who you met, what you can see. There is no need to use special words; normal, warm talk is what the baby needs to hear.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 2 months, would like support with the baby's language (talking and singing to the bump).
activity_name: Talking and Singing to the Baby During Pregnancy
activity_description: From around the second trimester, the parent and other family members talk, read aloud or sing to the baby in the womb for a few minutes each day. Use a calm voice and repeat the same songs or rhymes so the sounds become familiar. This also helps parents begin bonding before birth.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 2 months, would like support with the baby's language (talking and singing to the bump).
activity_name: Morning and Evening Greetings for the Baby
activity_description: Start and end each day by greeting the baby: say good morning, tell them what the day holds, and say goodnight before sleep. Place a hand on the bump while you talk if you like. Small, regular conversations help you bond and help the baby learn your voice.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 2 months, would like support with the baby's language (talking and singing to the bump).
activity_name: Father's Daily Words to the Baby
activity_description: Encourage the father to spend a few minutes each day talking or singing to the baby in the bump. Fathers who communicate early enjoy being involved from the very beginning.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 2 months, would like support with the baby's language (talking and singing to the bump).
activity_name: Reading a Story to the Bump
activity_description: Choose a short story, poem or passage and read it aloud to the baby for a few minutes each day, in a calm voice. Reading the same piece often helps the sounds become familiar. Partners and older children can take turns reading too.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 2 months, would like support with the baby's language (talking and singing to the bump).
activity_description: Caregivers are encouraged to gently massage the belly and speak softly during pregnancy, as touch and sound can be felt by the developing baby in later stages.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 4 months, would like support with bonding and emotional wellbeing.
activity_name: Talking and Singing to the Baby During Pregnancy
activity_description: From around the second trimester, the parent and other family members talk, read aloud or sing to the baby in the womb for a few minutes each day. Use a calm voice and repeat the same songs or rhymes so the sounds become familiar. This also helps parents begin bonding before birth.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 4 months, would like support with bonding and emotional wellbeing.
activity_name: Asking for Help with Household Work
activity_description: Sit down with your partner or family and list the household jobs that tire you most, such as carrying water or heavy laundry. Agree who will help with each. Accepting help lets you rest, eat well and look after your feelings, which all affect the baby.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 4 months, would like support with bonding and emotional wellbeing.
activity_name: End-of-Day Talk as a Couple or Family
activity_description: At the end of the day, spend a few minutes together talking about how the day went and planning for the next one, including how you will prepare for and care for the baby. Save any difficult conversations for a time when nobody is tired.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 4 months, would like support with bonding and emotional wellbeing.
activity_name: Father's Daily Words to the Baby
activity_description: Encourage the father to spend a few minutes each day talking or singing to the baby in the bump. Fathers who communicate early enjoy being involved from the very beginning.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 4 months, would like support with bonding and emotional wellbeing.
activity_name: Sharing Hopes and Worries About the Baby
activity_description: Take a few quiet minutes to think about how you feel about the baby's arrival, both the joys and the worries, and talk them over with someone you trust, such as your partner, a relative, a friend or your health worker at an antenatal visit. Talking it through can also help your family work out how they can support you. If worries feel heavy or do not ease, tell a health worker.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 4 months, would like support with bonding and emotional wellbeing.
activity_description: Build a short, regular relaxing routine into the day, such as a cup of tea, a chat with a friend or an easy walk, and ask family members to take on some household tasks so you can rest. Notice what helps you feel calm and keep doing it through the pregnancy. If you are unsure how much activity suits you, check with your health worker.

child_profile: Expecting parent, due in about 4 months, would like support with bonding and emotional wellbeing.
activity_description: When you feel the baby move or kick, pause and respond warmly: rest a hand on the spot, speak gently, and notice whether the baby moves again. A partner or another close adult can join in by feeling for movements and responding the same way, so both caregivers practise reading the baby's signals before birth.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet holding head up when on tummy (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: With the baby on their back, gently hold their ankles and move their legs in slow circles as if riding a bicycle. Say 'go' and 'stop' as you move.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet holding head up when on tummy (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Lean back comfortably and lay the baby tummy-down on your chest. Talk and smile so the baby lifts their head to look at you. This is a gentle way to start tummy time, especially for babies who dislike the floor.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet holding head up when on tummy (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: With the baby on their back, gently move their arms up and down and bicycle their legs while you sing or talk. Keep the movements slow and soft, and stop if the baby seems unhappy.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet holding head up when on tummy (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Draw the baby's attention to their feet. If they need help, give a small lift under their hips. Let them do as much as they can on their own.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet holding head up when on tummy (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Carry the baby tummy-down along your forearm, with their head supported in your hand and your other hand under their body. Walk around slowly so they can look about. Keep one hand on them at all times.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet holding head up when on tummy (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_name: Free Kicking Time on a Mat
activity_description: When the baby is awake, lay them on their back on a mat without tight wrapping so they can kick and wave their arms. Talk and play while they move. Short periods of free movement through the day are good for strength.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet holding head up when on tummy (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Lay the baby on a blanket with a few soft, safe toys nearby and encourage them to reach for, kick at, and bat the toys with their hands and feet.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet holding head up when on tummy (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_name: A Tummy Minute After Every Nappy Change
activity_description: After each nappy change, while the baby is awake and calm, place them on their tummy for a minute or two. Get down to their level and talk. Short, frequent sessions add up to more tummy time over the day. Always stay with the baby.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet holding head up when on tummy (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Set up a small, sturdy chair nearby. Use your voice or a toy to encourage the baby to climb into it. Let them play kneeling or turn and sit.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet holding head up when on tummy (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Lay the baby on their back facing you. Support behind their shoulders and head and slowly raise them to sitting, then lower them again. Once they hold their head well, practise holding their hands.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet holding head up when on tummy (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: While the baby is awake and an adult is watching, lay them on their stomach on a flat, firm surface. Start with one to two minutes a few times a day and lengthen sessions as the baby grows stronger. Get down at eye level, talk, or place a toy just in front of them to encourage lifting the head. Always place the baby on their back to sleep.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Sit face to face with the baby and smile. When they smile back, smile bigger and say something cheerful. Copy their expressions and sounds and wait for them to respond. Keep the game going as long as they enjoy it.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Hold the baby against your bare chest, with a light cover over you both if it is cool, so they can hear your voice and heartbeat and smell your scent. Keep the baby's face uncovered, and hold and comfort them often, especially when they are unsettled.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Hold and cuddle the baby often, and pick them up when they cry. Holding and responding to a young baby won't spoil them; it teaches them they are safe. Carrying the baby close during the day is a good way to do this.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Set aside some time each day when your phone is put away and you simply hold, look at and talk to the baby. Babies notice when you respond to them, and these focused moments help them feel connected to you.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_name: Smiles and Talk During Daily Care
activity_description: During feeds, baths and nappy changes, hold the baby close, look at them, smile and talk. Everyday care is full of chances to show love. Slow down a little and enjoy these moments together.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Notice what helps the baby calm down, such as sucking on their fingers or hands. Let them use these ways to settle, while staying close and comforting them when they need you. Over time they learn to calm themselves a little.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: During feeds, watch for signs that the baby has had enough, such as turning away, slowing down or closing their mouth. It is fine to stop when the baby isn't hungry. Responding to these signals helps them trust you.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Hold the baby close, make eye contact, and respond to their coos and sounds with matching sounds and facial expressions, pausing to let them 'reply.'

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Do something silly in front of the baby, such as dancing or acting out an animal with its sounds. Watch them follow your movements and smile.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Watch the baby closely during the day and notice the signals they give: looking at you when they want to play, turning away when they need a break, or rubbing their eyes when tired. Respond to what you see, and share what you learn with other carers.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Spend a few minutes face to face, smiling, laughing and talking with the baby. When they coo or smile, respond warmly and add more words. Copy their sounds now and then to get a conversation going.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: As the baby plays, say out loud what they are doing, for example that they are putting the blocks in, and show how pleased you are with their efforts. When they struggle, offer to do it together so they feel supported while still trying for themselves.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: During calm moments, walk slowly past the baby. When they try to get your attention with sounds or movements, stop, smile and talk to them.

child_profile: 2½ months old, not yet smiling when talked to or smiled at (most babies do by 2 months).
activity_description: Respond to the baby's cries, sounds and movements as soon as you can. Babies learn to trust that someone will pay attention to them, which builds a secure bond.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Spend a few minutes face to face, smiling, laughing and talking with the baby. When they coo or smile, respond warmly and add more words. Copy their sounds now and then to get a conversation going.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: When you go out with the baby, point out and name the new things you see: 'Look, a car!', 'That's a cow', 'See the tree?' Speak slowly and give them time to look. Everyday trips are full of words to share.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Go for a walk and let the baby hear the sounds around them. Talk about what you hear: 'Do you hear the birds singing? The wind is moving the leaves.'

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Every day, look at colourful pictures with the baby. Talk about what you see, and when the baby babbles, answer as if they are talking to you. Keep the back-and-forth going for as long as they enjoy it.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_name: A Quiet Time for Books and Songs
activity_description: Choose a quiet time each day, such as before a nap, to read or sing with the baby. Hold them close, keep your voice gentle and repeat favourite songs. A regular quiet time helps the baby settle and hear lots of language.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Sing to the baby several times a day, during baths, feeds or play, and play music they can listen to. Repeat the same songs often so they become familiar. Watch for the baby's smiles and sounds as they join in.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Sing songs that have hand movements, such as 'Wheels on the Bus', and do the actions for the baby. Watch for smiles and movements in response.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Make simple animal sounds (e.g., 'moo,' 'woof') near the baby in an animated voice, pausing to see if they respond with their own vocal sounds.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: During calm moments, walk slowly past the baby. When they try to get your attention with sounds or movements, stop, smile and talk to them.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Play with different sounds: whisper, clap, click your tongue, hum and make funny noises. Watch how the baby reacts and repeat the ones they like. Let other family members add their voices too.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Hold the baby so you can look into their eyes, and talk to them in your home language about what you are doing or seeing. Pause to let them answer with sounds or movements.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet making sounds back when talked to (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_name: Talking About What Baby Is Looking At
activity_description: Watch where the baby is looking and point to the same thing. Name it and say something about it: 'That's the cat. The cat is sleeping.' Following the baby's interest makes the words easier to learn.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Hold a baby-safe mirror in front of the child and narrate what they see, encouraging them to look, smile, and reach toward their reflection.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Pay attention to how the baby reacts to different things: songs, toys, people, being outside. Notice what makes them smile and what makes them fuss. Offer more of what they enjoy, and share what you learn with other carers.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Hide the child's favourite toys around the house and give clues to help them find them.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Push a few squares of colourful fabric into an empty wipes box or a tin with a smooth opening, leaving a corner showing. Show the baby how to pull one out, then let them try. Cheer each time a new colour appears, and refill the box together.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Show the baby a toy that moves or pops up, such as a wind-up toy. Let them watch it move again and again, and see their surprise.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Give the child time for free play where they choose what to do and use objects in new ways. Stay close but let them lead.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Sing to the baby several times a day, during baths, feeds or play, and play music they can listen to. Repeat the same songs often so they become familiar. Watch for the baby's smiles and sounds as they join in.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: When the baby drops a toy, pick it up, say 'Here it is!' and hand it back. Babies drop things on purpose to see what happens, so treat it as a game. Name what happened each time: 'Down it went! Back it comes!'

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Cover your head or a favorite toy with a light cloth and see if the baby pulls it away to find what is hidden underneath, repeating the game with excitement each time.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Lay the baby on their back and slowly move a bright-colored toy left to right and up and down at a comfortable distance, watching to see if the baby's eyes follow its movement.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_name: Simple Questions About What They See
activity_description: Ask simple questions about what the child can see: 'What's that?', 'Where is the dog?', 'What is Mama doing?' Give them time to answer by pointing or with words, and fill in the word if they need help.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Sit with the baby supported and show them how a soft ball rolls across the floor, drops from your hand and bounces. Let them touch and hold the balls. Say what each ball is doing as it moves.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_name: Reaching for a Ring on a String
activity_description: Tie a big, safe ring to a short piece of string. Hold it above the baby so they can see it, and move it slowly. Let them reach for it, touch it and pull it. Always hold the string yourself and put it away after play.

child_profile: 5 months old, not yet looking at their hands with interest (most babies do by 4 months).
activity_description: Give the baby an easy-to-hold cloth book or picture card with bright pictures. Let them hold it, look at it and mouth it. Point to the pictures and name them, and follow the baby's interest.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Take the child on a short walk outdoors, pausing to let them touch leaves, listen to sounds, and observe things like insects or clouds, naming what they notice together.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Play with different sounds: whisper, clap, click your tongue, hum and make funny noises. Watch how the baby reacts and repeat the ones they like. Let other family members add their voices too.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Use household items such as newspaper or a squeeze toy to make noises. Repeat sounds softly and a little louder (never too loud) and in different orders. Then help the baby make the sounds.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Introduce a few household items that produce different sounds and gently shake or crinkle them near the baby, pausing to watch their reaction and encourage turning toward the sound.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Pay attention to how the baby reacts to different things: songs, toys, people, being outside. Notice what makes them smile and what makes them fuss. Offer more of what they enjoy, and share what you learn with other carers.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Hand the baby a ball with different textures and see what they do. Show them how to roll it or drop it into a box.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Offer the baby clean, safe things to mouth, such as a teething ring, a large wooden spoon or a cloth. Babies learn about objects by mouthing them. Check that nothing is sharp, hot or small enough to choke on.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Gather pieces of fabric that feel different, such as soft cotton, knitted wool, rough denim and smooth satin. Let the baby touch each one with their hands and feet while you describe it: soft, rough, smooth.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Holding the baby securely, lift them slowly up and down, sway gently side to side and turn them to face different ways. Watch their face and slow down if they seem unsure. Keep movements smooth and gentle.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Hold the baby close and sway, bounce gently or dance slowly to music. Change the pace with different songs and watch how the baby responds. Keep the volume comfortable.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Place a few safe, clean objects with different textures within the baby's reach while they sit or lie on their tummy. Let them touch, hold and explore each item, and describe it: 'soft', 'rough', 'smooth'. Stay close by and check that every item is too large to be swallowed.

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Go for a walk and let the baby hear the sounds around them. Talk about what you hear: 'Do you hear the birds singing? The wind is moving the leaves.'

child_profile: 4½ months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the baby enjoys music and rattles.
activity_description: Sing to the baby several times a day, during baths, feeds or play, and play music they can listen to. Repeat the same songs often so they become familiar. Watch for the baby's smiles and sounds as they join in.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: While the baby stands holding a low surface, put toys lower down or on the floor so they squat to reach and stand back up. Celebrate each time they come up.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_name: Rolling Over to Reach a Toy
activity_description: During tummy time or back time, place a favourite toy just out of reach to one side. Encourage the baby to reach and roll towards it, and cheer every effort. Let them get the toy in the end so it stays fun.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: Offer soft, small pieces of safe food for the baby to pick up and feed themselves. Expect mess, and stay with them throughout. Avoid foods that are choking hazards, such as whole groundnuts or hard raw pieces.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: Place the baby on their tummy or back with a toy just out of reach, and gently encourage them to roll over or stretch to reach it, celebrating when they succeed.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_name: Passing a Spoon from Hand to Hand
activity_description: Give the baby a wooden spoon in one hand and show them how to pass it to the other. Offer it to alternate hands. Praise each try and let them explore the spoon in their own way.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: With the baby sitting, place toys in front of them, then slowly move them to the side so the baby reaches across their body.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: Arrange cushions or soft household items into a simple path and encourage the child to crawl over and around them under close supervision.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: If the baby can't yet roll over alone, hold one leg and slowly guide them through rolling onto their tummy. Practise rolling to both sides.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: Set up a small, sturdy chair nearby. Use your voice or a toy to encourage the baby to climb into it. Let them play kneeling or turn and sit.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: Make sure the baby has sturdy, stable furniture they can safely pull up on, such as a low table or sofa. Place a toy on top to encourage them. Stay close and remove anything that could tip over or fall.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: Place toys in a large circle on the floor and lay the baby tummy-down in the middle. Watch them reach and move around to play.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: Give the child a soft ball to kick, roll, and throw back and forth, encouraging them to try each movement in a safe open space.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: Blow up a beach ball so it is a little soft. Hold the baby carefully tummy-down on top and roll them slowly back and forth and side to side.

child_profile: 8 months old, not yet rolling from tummy to back (most babies do by 6 months).
activity_description: Draw the baby's attention to their feet. If they need help, give a small lift under their hips. Let them do as much as they can on their own.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: Place toys in a large circle on the floor and lay the baby tummy-down in the middle. Watch them reach and move around to play.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: When the baby makes a sound like 'ba', repeat it and add a simple word: 'Ba! Ball!' Repeat the sounds they make and keep adding words that match. Smile and wait for them to try again.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: Use the baby's name often when you talk to them, keeping your voice calm and gentle and smiling warmly. Sing softly, and avoid sudden loud sounds, which can upset babies.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: Watch what the baby does and copy them. If they bang a block or clap, do the same. Let them lead the play.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: As the baby plays, say out loud what they are doing, for example that they are putting the blocks in, and show how pleased you are with their efforts. When they struggle, offer to do it together so they feel supported while still trying for themselves.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: During calm moments, walk slowly past the baby. When they try to get your attention with sounds or movements, stop, smile and talk to them.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: Hold the baby close, about 20 to 25 cm from your face, and smile. Change the tone of your voice to get their attention. When they are calm and looking at you, it is time to play.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: When the baby makes a sound, copy it back to them and pause to let them respond, building a simple back-and-forth exchange similar to conversation.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: Sit face to face with the baby and smile. When they smile back, smile bigger and say something cheerful. Copy their expressions and sounds and wait for them to respond. Keep the game going as long as they enjoy it.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: Face the baby, cover your face with your hands or a light cloth, then uncover it while saying 'peekaboo' with a smile. Pause to let the baby react, and repeat. As the baby gets older, let them pull the cloth away or hide their own face.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: When you need to leave the baby with someone, say a short, cheerful goodbye rather than slipping away. When you come back, greet them warmly and tell them you're back. This builds trust that you return.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: Make simple facial expressions such as smiling, surprise, or puckering lips, and encourage the child to copy them back, responding warmly to their attempts.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: Clap with excitement when the baby does something good and encourage them to clap with you.

child_profile: 11 months old, not yet smiling or laughing at peek-a-boo (most babies do by 9 months).
activity_description: Hold a baby-safe mirror in front of the child and narrate what they see, encouraging them to look, smile, and reach toward their reflection.

activity_description: Place the baby on their tummy or back with a toy just out of reach, and gently encourage them to roll over or stretch to reach it, celebrating when they succeed.

activity_description: Sing to the baby several times a day, during baths, feeds or play, and play music they can listen to. Repeat the same songs often so they become familiar. Watch for the baby's smiles and sounds as they join in.

child_profile: 7 months old and on track: laughs and rolls from tummy to back; no concerns.
activity_description: As you do chores, point to objects and say what you are doing. Help the baby point with their finger and give them something safe to hold, like a wet cloth.

child_profile: 7 months old and on track: laughs and rolls from tummy to back; no concerns.
activity_description: Sing songs that have hand movements, such as 'Wheels on the Bus', and do the actions for the baby. Watch for smiles and movements in response.

child_profile: 7 months old and on track: laughs and rolls from tummy to back; no concerns.
activity_description: Place toys in a large circle on the floor and lay the baby tummy-down in the middle. Watch them reach and move around to play.

child_profile: 7 months old and on track: laughs and rolls from tummy to back; no concerns.
activity_description: As the baby plays, say out loud what they are doing, for example that they are putting the blocks in, and show how pleased you are with their efforts. When they struggle, offer to do it together so they feel supported while still trying for themselves.

child_profile: 7 months old and on track: laughs and rolls from tummy to back; no concerns.
activity_description: Place a few safe, clean objects with different textures within the baby's reach while they sit or lie on their tummy. Let them touch, hold and explore each item, and describe it: 'soft', 'rough', 'smooth'. Stay close by and check that every item is too large to be swallowed.

child_profile: 7 months old and on track: laughs and rolls from tummy to back; no concerns.
activity_description: Take the child on a short walk outdoors, pausing to let them touch leaves, listen to sounds, and observe things like insects or clouds, naming what they notice together.

child_profile: 7 months old and on track: laughs and rolls from tummy to back; no concerns.
activity_description: Face the baby, cover your face with your hands or a light cloth, then uncover it while saying 'peekaboo' with a smile. Pause to let the baby react, and repeat. As the baby gets older, let them pull the cloth away or hide their own face.

child_profile: 7 months old and on track: laughs and rolls from tummy to back; no concerns.
activity_description: Arrange cushions or soft household items into a simple path and encourage the child to crawl over and around them under close supervision.

child_profile: 7 months old and on track: laughs and rolls from tummy to back; no concerns.
activity_description: Go for a walk and let the baby hear the sounds around them. Talk about what you hear: 'Do you hear the birds singing? The wind is moving the leaves.'

child_profile: 14 months old, not yet waving bye-bye or calling a parent mama or dada (most children do by 12 months).
activity_description: Look at a picture book or magazine together and name the objects you see as you point to them, pausing to let the child attempt the word before you repeat it clearly.

activity_description: Hold a soft toy and pretend it is talking to the child: 'Hello! What are you eating?' Give the child their own toy and see if they talk back or copy you. Keep the voices playful.

child_profile: 14 months old, not yet waving bye-bye or calling a parent mama or dada (most children do by 12 months).
activity_description: Talk through daily routines as you do them and make up short songs about them: a washing-hands song, a getting-dressed song. Use the same songs every day so the child learns the words.

activity_description: Hold the baby so you can look into their eyes, and talk to them in your home language about what you are doing or seeing. Pause to let them answer with sounds or movements.

activity_description: When the child points to something, name it, then wait a few seconds to see if they make a sound. Whatever sound they make, respond warmly and say the name again.

child_profile: 14 months old, not yet waving bye-bye or calling a parent mama or dada (most children do by 12 months).
activity_description: Make a simple book with photos of family members, friends and pets, including one of the child. Look at it together and name each person. Ask 'Where's Shosho?' and let them point.

child_profile: 14 months old, not yet waving bye-bye or calling a parent mama or dada (most children do by 12 months).
activity_description: Speak to the child simply using real words rather than baby talk. Give short directions like 'Roll the ball' and show them what you mean.

child_profile: 14 months old, not yet waving bye-bye or calling a parent mama or dada (most children do by 12 months).
activity_description: Show the baby simple gestures and use them every day: wave bye-bye when someone leaves, shake your head for 'no', clap when something is good. Say the word as you do the gesture and help them copy.

child_profile: 14 months old, not yet waving bye-bye or calling a parent mama or dada (most children do by 12 months).
activity_description: When the child says a word or part of a word, repeat it clearly and add a little more. If they say 'ba', say 'Ball! A red ball!' Keep your words simple, and smile to show you understood them.

child_profile: 14 months old, not yet waving bye-bye or calling a parent mama or dada (most children do by 12 months).
activity_description: During daily routines, point to an object the child is looking at and name it clearly, for example 'cup' while at mealtime. Repeat the word several times, wait for the child to look, point or try the word, and respond warmly to any attempt. Gradually add simple describing words such as 'big cup' or 'red ball'.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Play simple matching games, such as putting shapes into a sorter or fitting large puzzle pieces. Help at first, then let them try on their own.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Arrange sturdy furniture, such as a sofa and a low table, so the child can hold on and step sideways along it. Place a toy at one end to encourage them. Stay close and remove anything that could tip.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Give the child time for free play where they choose what to do and use objects in new ways. Stay close but let them lead.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Join in pretend play, such as rocking a teddy to sleep or singing into a wooden spoon as a microphone. Take turns so the child copies and leads.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Give the child a clean container and a handful of clothes pegs. Show them how to drop the pegs in and tip them out again. As they get better, cut a slot in a plastic lid for posting the pegs through.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_name: Simple Questions About What They See
activity_description: Ask simple questions about what the child can see: 'What's that?', 'Where is the dog?', 'What is Mama doing?' Give them time to answer by pointing or with words, and fill in the word if they need help.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Show the child an everyday object, such as a hat, and show how it is used by putting it on your head. Hand it to them and see if they copy you. Try other objects like a comb or a cup, and cheer their attempts.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Hide the child's favourite toys around the house and give clues to help them find them.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Gather two or three kinds of objects, such as cups, socks and spoons. Show the child how to put the same things together, then let them try. Ask them to hand you a certain object: 'Can you give me the spoon?'

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Sit with the child and take turns dumping blocks or safe small objects out of a container and putting them back in, narrating the action as you play together.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Put funny hats on yourselves and look in the mirror together. Do a little dance and talk about what you are wearing.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: As the child walks more confidently, ask them to carry light objects from one place to another.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Sit with the child and show how to stack two or three blocks, then invite them to try. Celebrate when the tower stands, and let them knock it down to see what happens. Increase the number of blocks as their skill improves, and talk about 'up', 'down', 'on top' and 'fall'.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Give the child three or four cups or containers of different sizes. Show them how the small ones fit inside the big ones, then take them out again. Let them try, and talk about big and small as they play.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Let the child help open drawers and doors, such as when putting clothes away or going outside.

child_profile: 16 months old, not yet stacking two small objects like blocks (most children do by 15 months).
activity_description: Read a book with flaps to lift or textures to touch, and let the child find what is under each flap. Talk about the pictures. If you don't have one, glue paper flaps over pictures in a homemade book.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.
activity_description: Take the baby outside and let them touch leaves and grass safely. Talk about what they touch, smell, see and hear: 'The rock feels hard.'

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.
activity_description: Fill a bucket with blocks or objects of different sizes, textures and colours, all too big to swallow. Let the child take them out, feel them and put them back. Describe each one as they explore.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.
activity_description: Blow bubbles for the child to watch, reach for and pop. Name what happens: 'Up, up! Pop!' Keep the mixture out of their mouth and eyes.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.
activity_description: Read books with different textures and let the child touch them. Use words for what they feel: rough, bumpy, soft.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.
activity_description: Take the child on a short walk outdoors, pausing to let them touch leaves, listen to sounds, and observe things like insects or clouds, naming what they notice together.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.
activity_description: Set out pots, lids, wooden spoons and sealed bottle shakers. Let the child bang, shake and tap them, and show them how to play loudly and softly. Join in with a song.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.
activity_description: Cover a table with plastic and spread a little shaving cream or thick soap foam on it. Let the child squish it, draw in it and explore with their hands, brushes or spoons. Keep it away from their eyes and mouth, and wash hands afterwards.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.
activity_description: Point to interesting things around you, such as a bird, a car or a cow, and say 'Look!' Wait for the child to follow your finger and look. Name what you see together and talk about it.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.
activity_description: Take the child to a sandpit or beach with a small spade and bucket and let them dig and pour.

child_profile: 13 months old; the caregiver would like support with sensory development; the child enjoys water play and sand.
activity_description: On outings such as a bus or matatu ride, a walk or a market visit, point out new sights, sounds and smells. Ask the child what they can see and hear. Encourage their questions and curiosity.

child_profile: 15½ months old, not yet taking a few steps alone or showing affection with hugs (most children do both by 15 months).

child_profile: 15½ months old, not yet taking a few steps alone or showing affection with hugs (most children do both by 15 months).
activity_description: During daily routines, name the child's apparent emotions out loud (e.g., 'you seem happy,' 'that felt frustrating') to help them begin associating words with feelings.

child_profile: 15½ months old, not yet taking a few steps alone or showing affection with hugs (most children do both by 15 months).

child_profile: 15½ months old, not yet taking a few steps alone or showing affection with hugs (most children do both by 15 months).

child_profile: 15½ months old, not yet taking a few steps alone or showing affection with hugs (most children do both by 15 months).
activity_description: Hold the child's hands and encourage them to walk along a line taped on the floor or a low, stable wooden plank, supporting balance as needed.
